intro.en: Comprehensive guide to intrapartum electronic fetal monitoring covering equipment, DR C BRAVADO interpretation framework, physiological abnormalities, and NICE/RCOG clinical management guidelines.

items.summary: Continuous electronic apparatus used to simultaneously record fetal cardiac activity and uterine contractions throughout antepartum surveillance and active labour.

blocks.title: Components and mechanism
bullets: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring records fetal heart rate alongside uterine muscular contractions.
Ultrasound Doppler transducer placed over the maternal abdomen detects moving cardiac valves, calculating heart rate via autocorrelation.
Tocodynamometer pressure transducer positioned over the uterine fundus detects changes in abdominal wall displacement during contractions.
Dual-channel recording console prints fetal heart rate in the upper pane and uterine tone in the lower pane on calibrated paper moving at standard speed.
Maternal event marker button allows the pregnant woman to flag perceived fetal movements, producing an upward deflection on the paper printout.

groups.label: Antenatal maternal risk factors
bullets: Pre-existing diabetes mellitus or gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
Chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, or pre-eclampsia.
Previous lower segment caesarean section (LSCS).
Recurrent antepartum haemorrhage (APH).
Maternal obesity with body mass index > 35 kg/m2.
Prolonged pre-labour rupture of membranes.

groups.label: Antenatal fetal risk factors
bullets: Multiple pregnancy (twins, higher-order multiples).
Fetal growth restriction (IUGR/FGR).
Polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios.
Breech presentation or unstable fetal lie.
Maternally reported reduced fetal movements over the preceding 24 hours.

groups.label: Intrapartum risk factors
bullets: Augmented or induced labour with intravenous oxytocin.
Labour following epidural analgesia.
Fresh vaginal bleeding presenting during labour.
Maternal pyrexia or unexplained maternal tachycardia.
Suspected chorioamnionitis or intra-amniotic infection.
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid.
Abnormal fetal heart rate auscultated via Pinard stethoscope or handheld Doppler.

groups.label: Advantages
bullets: Straightforward to execute with minimal operator preparation.
Provides continuous permanent graphic documentation valuable for medico-legal verification.
Associated with a significant decrease in the occurrence of early neonatal seizures.

groups.label: Disadvantages and limitations
bullets: Time consuming and restricts maternal ambulation during continuous recording.
High false-positive rate of roughly 70% for predicting fetal hypoxia.
Low clinical specificity for true fetal acidosis, leading to unnecessary caesarean births.
Generates parental anxiety and distress regarding fetal status.
Highly subjective visual analysis with wide inter-observer and intra-observer inconsistency.
Cannot anticipate abrupt cataclysmic events such as cord prolapse or uterine rupture.
Weak association with long-term childhood neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Provides limited clinical benefit without adjunct fetal blood sampling (FBS) facilities.

viva.q: What two physiological parameters does a cardiotocograph monitor simultaneously?
viva.a: It records the fetal heart rate using a pulsed Doppler ultrasound transducer and the frequency and duration of uterine contractions using an external tocodynamometer.

viva.q: Why is internal cardiotocography contraindicated in a mother who is seropositive for HIV or Hepatitis B?
viva.a: Attaching the spiral fetal scalp electrode causes microscopic breach of the fetal epidermis, markedly escalating the risk of vertical pathogen transmission to the fetus.

viva.q: What is the principal clinical disadvantage of continuous intrapartum electronic fetal monitoring?
viva.a: It has an elevated false-positive rate of approximately 70% for fetal hypoxaemia, which increases operative interventions without improving long-term neurological outcomes.

title.en: Systematic CTG interpretation: DR C BRAVADO method

items.summary: Structured assessment mnemonic devised by Advanced Life Support in Obstetrics (ALSO) ensuring rigorous, sequential evaluation of intrapartum cardiotocograph traces.

blocks.title: The DR C BRAVADO framework
bullets: D (Define): Establish the baseline clinical context, reason for monitoring, and verify paper speed calibration.
R (Risk): Determine whether the pregnancy has antenatal or intrapartum high-risk or low-risk characteristics.
C (Contractions): Count uterine contractions across a 10-minute window, noting frequency, duration, strength, and resting tone.
B (Baseline): Establish the average resting fetal heart rate over a 10-minute window between contractions, ignoring accelerations and decelerations.
R (Rate): Check that baseline resting rate falls within the normal physiological bracket of 100 to 160 beats per minute.
V (Variability): Measure the amplitude of minor beat-to-beat baseline fluctuations over a 1-minute interval (normal > 5 bpm).
A (Accelerations): Identify transient heart rate increases above baseline, reflecting a healthy, neurologically responsive fetus.
D (Decelerations): Detect episodic transient dips below baseline rate and classify their timing (early, late, variable, or prolonged).
O (Overall assessment): Synthesize all physiological features into a final clinical judgment (reassuring, non-reassuring, or abnormal) to formulate the plan.

blocks.title: Clinical points to remember
bullets: A cardiotocograph trace should never be judged in isolation; it must be interpreted alongside maternal observations, labour progress, and parity.
Contraction frequency is recorded as the number of contractions per 10 minutes; tachysystole is defined as more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes.
Baseline rate determination requires a stable trace segment of at least 10 minutes free from contractions and episodic changes.

viva.q: What does the mnemonic DR C BRAVADO stand for in CTG interpretation?
viva.a: Define, Risk, Contractions, Baseline Rate, Variability, Accelerations, Decelerations, and Overall assessment.

viva.q: How is uterine contraction frequency evaluated under the DR C BRAVADO approach?
viva.a: Contraction frequency is quantified as the total number of contractions occurring over a rolling 10-minute period; normal labour typically demonstrates 3 to 4 contractions per 10 minutes.

viva.q: Why is the final letter O in DR C BRAVADO critical?
viva.a: Overall assessment requires the clinician to combine all separate features into a definitive category and establish a prompt management plan.

title.en: Baseline fetal heart rate and abnormalities

items.summary: Evaluation of the resting mean fetal heart rate between uterine contractions, identifying normal physiological ranges and the differential diagnosis of baseline tachycardia and bradycardia.

blocks.title: Normal baseline rate and definitions
bullets: Normal resting baseline rate ranges between 100 and 160 beats per minute (bpm).
Baseline tachycardia is defined as a resting heart rate sustained above 160 bpm for at least 10 minutes.
Severe baseline tachycardia is defined as a resting heart rate exceeding 180 bpm.
Baseline bradycardia is defined as a resting heart rate sustained below 100 bpm for at least 10 minutes.
A single prolonged deceleration exceeding 3 minutes in duration is classified as acute fetal bradycardia.

groups.label: Maternal causes
bullets: Maternal fever or chorioamnionitis and systemic sepsis.
Maternal dehydration or prolonged ketosis in labour.
Maternal psychological anxiety or severe acute pain.
Maternal chronic or acute anaemia.
Maternal hyperthyroidism or thyroid storm.
Incidental maternal tachycardia.
Epidural analgesia.
Medications, notably beta-sympathomimetic tocolytics such as ritodrine hydrochloride, and anticholinergic agents.

groups.label: Fetal causes
bullets: Early fetal hypoxia and hypoxaemia triggering compensatory sympathetic stimulation.
Extreme prematurity due to incomplete parasympathetic cardiac autonomic maturation.
Fetal tachyarrhythmias (such as supraventricular tachycardia).
Decompensated congestive cardiac failure.
Fetal anaemia secondary to isoimmunisation or feto-maternal hemorrhage.
Vigorous active fetal somatic movements.

groups.label: Maternal causes
bullets: Maternal supine hypotensive syndrome due to inferior vena cava compression.
Acute systemic hypotension following epidural or spinal sympathetic blockade.
Maternal epileptic seizures or eclamptic convulsions.
Post-dated or post-term gestation.
Local anaesthetic toxicity following paracervical infiltration or accidental intravenous entry.
Administration of narcotic analgesic agents.

groups.label: Fetal causes
bullets: Severe, prolonged, or decompensated fetal hypoxia and metabolic acidosis.
Acute umbilical cord prolapse or prolonged cord occlusion.
Congenital complete atrioventricular heart block, frequently associated with maternal autoimmune anti-Ro/SSA antibodies.
Sustained fetal head compression during late second stage of labour.
Occipitoposterior malposition.
Transverse or oblique fetal lie.

blocks.title: Clinical points to remember
bullets: Tachycardia accompanied by reduced variability and decelerations indicates progressive fetal metabolic acidaemia.
Isolated mild tachycardia with normal variability and accelerations is usually maternal pyrexia or dehydration; rehydrate and administer paracetamol.
Acute bradycardia lasting over 3 minutes requires immediate intrauterine resuscitation and urgent preparations for operative delivery.

viva.q: What is the normal baseline fetal heart rate range on an intrapartum CTG?
viva.a: The physiological baseline heart rate is 100 to 160 beats per minute established over a 10-minute segment free from uterine contractions.

viva.q: Which maternal medications commonly cause fetal baseline tachycardia?
viva.a: Beta-sympathomimetics such as ritodrine hydrochloride and terbutaline, and anticholinergic drugs like atropine cause fetal tachycardia through transplacental adrenergic stimulation.

viva.q: What cardiac abnormality should be suspected when persistent fetal bradycardia occurs with completely normal variability?
viva.a: Congenital complete atrioventricular heart block, frequently linked to maternal autoimmune conditions with anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies.

items.summary: Analysis of the minor beat-to-beat fluctuations in the baseline fetal heart rate reflecting sympathetic-parasympathetic autonomic equilibrium and fetal cerebral oxygenation.

blocks.title: Normal variability and classification
bullets: Baseline variability denotes the amplitude bandwidth of minor heart rate fluctuations recorded across a 1-minute window, excluding accelerations and decelerations.
Normal variability is defined as an amplitude of greater than 5 beats per minute (> 5 bpm), demonstrating an intact autonomic nervous system.
Reduced (non-reassuring) variability is defined as an amplitude of less than 5 bpm (< 5 bpm) lasting between 30 and 90 minutes.
Absent or severely reduced (abnormal) variability is defined as an amplitude of less than 5 bpm persisting for greater than 90 minutes (or > 30 minutes in the presence of decelerations).
Saltatory (exaggerated) variability denotes an excessively wide amplitude bandwidth, which may indicate acute fetal autonomic instability or cord compression.

groups.label: Maternal pharmacological causes
bullets: Central nervous system depressants including opioids (pethidine, morphine).
Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam).
Magnesium sulphate (MgSO4) administered for pre-eclampsia or eclampsia neuroprotection.
General anaesthetic inhalation agents.
Local anaesthetics (paracervical or epidural infiltration).

groups.label: Fetal physiological causes
bullets: Normal fetal quiet sleep state (typically resolving spontaneously within a brief resting episode).
Prematurity with immature development of the cardiac autonomic pacemakers and vagal pathways.

groups.label: Fetal pathological causes
bullets: Fetal cerebral hypoxia and advancing metabolic acidosis causing central depression.
Structural central nervous system malformations or intracranial trauma.
Congenital cardiac structural malformations.
Antecedent neurological injury or impending intrauterine fetal demise.

blocks.title: Clinical points to remember
bullets: Normal baseline variability (> 5 bpm) is the most reassuring feature on a CTG, reliably confirming that the fetus is non-acidotic.
Reduced variability persisting beyond an ordinary resting episode without maternal sedation is unlikely to be physiological sleep; reassessment and stimulation are indicated.
The combination of reduced variability (< 5 bpm) and late or atypical variable decelerations denotes severe fetal metabolic acidaemia requiring urgent delivery.

viva.q: What is the normal baseline variability on an intrapartum CTG?
viva.a: Normal baseline variability is greater than 5 beats per minute over a 1-minute trace interval, confirming intact cerebral oxygenation.

viva.q: How does a normal fetal sleep cycle differ clinically from pathological reduced variability?
viva.a: Fetal sleep produces reduced variability that is transient and resolves spontaneously; pathological depression persists and is accompanied by decelerations.

viva.q: Which maternal drugs frequently cause transient loss of fetal heart rate variability?
viva.a: Central nervous system depressants including pethidine, morphine, diazepam, and magnesium sulphate readily cross the placenta and suppress variability.

items.summary: Symmetrical, gradual transient dips in fetal heart rate coinciding synchronously with uterine contractions, caused by physiological compression of the fetal head.

blocks.title: Morphology and characteristics
bullets: Symmetrical, gradual decline in fetal heart rate that forms the exact mirror image of the uterine contraction curve.
Synchronised onset: the heart rate begins falling concurrently with the commencement of the uterine contraction.
Concordant nadir: the lowest point (nadir) of the heart rate dip coincides precisely with the peak (acme) of the uterine contraction.
Prompt recovery: the fetal heart rate recovers fully back to baseline by the end of the contraction.
Preserved inter-contraction baseline: normal resting baseline rate and normal variability (> 5 bpm) are maintained between contractions.

blocks.title: Pathophysiology and timing
bullets: Mechanical pressure against the fetal skull during uterine contractions increases intracranial pressure, eliciting vagal parasympathetic discharge and reflex bradycardia.
The reflex slows cardiac pacing without causing tissue hypoxaemia or metabolic acidosis.
Typically observed in the late first stage of labour and early second stage as the presenting part engages and descends into the pelvic canal.

blocks.title: Clinical implications and management
bullets: Considered physiological and uncomplicated when resting baseline rate and baseline variability remain reassuring.
Does not signify fetal hypoxaemia or acidosis; immediate operative intervention or delivery is not required.
Continue regular cardiotocographic surveillance while checking for physical impediment to fetal descent, such as a distended maternal bladder.

viva.q: What is the physiological mechanism responsible for early decelerations?
viva.a: Mechanical compression of the fetal head increases intracranial pressure and stimulates the vagus nerve, causing a transient benign reflex bradycardia that mirrors the contraction.

viva.q: How can an examiner differentiate an early deceleration from a late deceleration on a CTG printout?
viva.a: In an early deceleration, the nadir aligns with the contraction peak and recovers with contraction offset; in a late deceleration, the nadir and recovery lag after the contraction.

viva.q: What clinical intervention is indicated when early decelerations are noted in labour with normal variability?
viva.a: Immediate intervention is not needed; continue routine CTG monitoring and confirm that maternal bladder distension is not obstructing descending presenting part.

items.summary: Gradual transient decreases in fetal heart rate lagging after uterine contractions, characteristically reflecting compromised uteroplacental perfusion and fetal hypoxaemia.

blocks.title: Morphology and characteristics
bullets: Typically exhibits a broad, shallow, symmetrical U-shaped contour.
Delayed onset: the heart rate starts declining after the uterine contraction has already commenced.
Delayed nadir: the lowest point (nadir) of the deceleration occurs after the peak of the uterine contraction.
Delayed offset: the fetal heart rate does not return to baseline until well after the uterine contraction has ceased.
Prolonged recovery: the deceleration takes substantially longer to resolve compared to a physiological early deceleration.
Late decelerations occurring in > 50% of contractions for up to 30 minutes are non-reassuring; persisting over 30 minutes is abnormal.

blocks.title: Etiology
bullets: Maternal hypotension: supine inferior vena caval compression (supine hypotensive syndrome), sympathetic vasomotor blockade following epidural analgesia.
Uteroplacental insufficiency: fetal growth restriction (IUGR), placental abruption, post-term pregnancy, maternal vascular disease.
Uterine tachysystole / hyperstimulation: excessive intravenous oxytocin titration or prostaglandin (PGE2) administration leading to inadequate intervillous recovery.

blocks.title: Clinical implications and intrauterine resuscitation
bullets: Notify the consultant obstetrician immediately; structured monitoring and prompt intrauterine resuscitation are mandatory.
Position the mother in the full left lateral tilt to relieve aortocaval compression and optimize venous return.
Administer an intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus; if hypotension persists after epidural, use vasopressors such as intravenous ephedrine.
Reduce or immediately stop intravenous oxytocin infusion.
Administer acute tocolytic therapy (such as subcutaneous terbutaline) if uterine hyperstimulation or hypertonus is present.
Perform fetal blood sampling (FBS) or prepare for expedited delivery within 30 minutes if late decelerations fail to resolve.

viva.q: What is the pathological mechanism producing late decelerations in labour?
viva.a: Uteroplacental insufficiency causes transient fetal hypoxaemia during contractions, triggering chemoreceptor-mediated vagal bradycardia and direct myocardial depression lagging behind the contraction.

viva.q: What are the first three immediate steps in intrauterine resuscitation for late decelerations?
viva.a: Turn the mother onto her left side, discontinue any oxytocin infusion immediately, and administer a rapid intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus.

viva.q: What threshold defines late decelerations as abnormal rather than non-reassuring?
viva.a: Late decelerations occurring in > 50% of contractions persisting for over 30 minutes and failing to respond to conservative resuscitation are classified as abnormal.

items.summary: Abrupt, episodic decreases in fetal heart rate showing variable morphology and timing unrelated to uterine contractions, primarily caused by transient umbilical cord compression.

blocks.title: Morphology and defining features
bullets: Displays variable, inconsistent contour, depth, and duration with no constant relationship to uterine contractions.
Characterized by rapid descent (< 30 seconds to nadir) and rapid recovery, often flanked by compensatory accelerations ('shoulders').
Uncomplicated variable decelerations: heart rate drops by < 60 bpm and takes < 60 seconds to recover, with preserved baseline variability.
Non-reassuring variable decelerations: drop < 60 bpm and recovery < 60 seconds lasting up to 30 minutes (or > 90 minutes) in > 50% of contractions; or drop >= 60 bpm and recovery >= 60 seconds.
Abnormal variable decelerations: non-reassuring variable decelerations persisting after 30 minutes of conservative treatment in > 50% of contractions.

blocks.title: Etiology
bullets: Mechanical compression of the umbilical cord between the fetal body and the uterine wall during contractions or movements.
Overt umbilical cord prolapse or occult cord presentation.
Nuchal cord (umbilical cord coiled snugly around the fetal neck).
Severe oligohydramnios resulting in loss of protective amniotic fluid buffer.
Reduced Wharton's jelly volume within the umbilical cord sheath, predisposing vessels to collapse.

blocks.title: Management and clinical escalation
bullets: Notify the consultant obstetrician; structured clinical assessment and management are required.
Perform urgent sterile vaginal examination to inspect and palpate for umbilical cord prolapse.
Change maternal posture (left lateral, right lateral, or knee-chest position) to relieve cord entrapment.
Consider amnioinfusion in labour complicated by severe oligohydramnios and persistent variable decelerations.
Perform fetal blood sampling (FBS) to check acid-base status or expedite delivery if decelerations become atypical and persistent.

viva.q: What is the primary etiology of variable decelerations on a CTG?
viva.a: Transient umbilical cord compression, which abruptly increases fetal systemic vascular resistance, stimulating baroreceptors and triggering rapid vagal reflex bradycardia.

viva.q: What features distinguish an uncomplicated variable deceleration from an atypical one?
viva.a: Uncomplicated decelerations drop by < 60 bpm, recover in < 60 seconds, and retain baseline variability; atypical decelerations drop >= 60 bpm, take >= 60 seconds, or lose variability.

viva.q: What initial clinical examination must be performed when severe variable decelerations suddenly appear?
viva.a: An immediate sterile vaginal examination to exclude umbilical cord prolapse or occult presentation below the descending fetal head.

title.en: Categorisation of fetal heart rate features (NICE and RCOG)

items.summary: Standardised clinical reference matrix categorising baseline heart rate, baseline variability, and decelerations into reassuring, non-reassuring, and abnormal tiers based on NICE and RCOG guidelines.

blocks.title: Fetal heart rate feature classification matrix

head: Feature
Normal / Reassuring
Non-reassuring
Abnormal
rows: Baseline fetal heart rate (bpm)
Baseline variability (bpm)
< 5 lasting for 30 to 90 minutes
< 5 lasting for > 30 minutes (or persistent)
Decelerations
None OR early decelerations
Variable decelerations with drop < 60 bpm, recovery < 60s in > 50% contractions; or late decelerations up to 30 min in > 50% contractions
Persistent non-reassuring variable decelerations after 30 min treatment in > 50% contractions; late decelerations > 30 min; or single prolonged deceleration > 3 minutes

blocks.title: Evaluation of accelerations
bullets: Accelerations are defined as transient increases in fetal heart rate above baseline.
The presence of accelerations in an intrapartum trace is a reassuring sign of fetal autonomic stability and absence of metabolic acidosis.
The absence of accelerations in an otherwise normal intrapartum cardiotocograph is not by itself predictive of fetal hypoxaemia or acidosis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Single prolonged deceleration lasting greater than 3 minutes is categorized as abnormal and mandates immediate intrauterine resuscitation and preparations for delivery.
Reassessment must occur whenever clinical parameters change or conservative corrective maneuvers are introduced.
Individual feature grading forms the basis for overall trace categorization into reassuring, suspicious, or pathological states.

viva.q: How is baseline fetal heart rate categorized under RCOG and NICE guidelines?
viva.a: Normal is 100 to 160 bpm; non-reassuring is 161 to 180 bpm; abnormal is either baseline tachycardia > 180 bpm or baseline bradycardia < 100 bpm.

viva.q: What duration of baseline variability < 5 bpm upgrades the feature from non-reassuring to abnormal?
viva.a: Variability < 5 bpm lasting 30 to 90 minutes is non-reassuring; if it persists beyond 90 minutes (or > 30 minutes with decelerations), it is categorized as abnormal.

viva.q: What is the clinical significance of absent accelerations on an otherwise normal intrapartum CTG?
viva.a: In labour, the absence of accelerations on an otherwise normal trace is common and does not by itself indicate fetal acidosis or hypoxaemia.

title.en: Categorisation of CTG traces and clinical management (NICE and RCOG)

items.summary: Integrated classification algorithm synthesizing individual fetal heart rate features to grade overall cardiotocograph traces into normal, suspicious, and pathological tiers with mandated clinical interventions.

blocks.title: Trace categorization and clinical management algorithm

head: Category
Criteria / Feature combination
Clinical interpretation and action plan
rows: Normal / Reassuring
All three features (baseline rate, variability, decelerations) are normal/reassuring
Normal CTG pattern indicating a healthy fetus; continue standard CTG monitoring and routine intrapartum care.
Non-reassuring / Suspicious
One feature is non-reassuring and two features are normal/reassuring
Increased risk of acidosis; identify causes, give IV fluids, left lateral tilt, paracetamol for fever, reduce or stop oxytocin, inform consultant.
Abnormal / Pathological
One feature is abnormal OR two features are non-reassuring
Significant acidosis risk; urgent resuscitation, fluids, lateral tilt, stop oxytocin, consider tocolytics, offer FBS, act within 30 min, expedite delivery.

blocks.title: Principles of intrauterine resuscitation
bullets: Turn mother onto her left side to eliminate aortocaval compression and maximize uteroplacental blood flow.
Administer an intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus to correct dehydration and hypovolaemia.
Discontinue or reduce oxytocin infusion immediately to alleviate uterine hyperstimulation and restore intervillous perfusion.
Administer antipyretic medication (intravenous or oral paracetamol) in cases of maternal pyrexia.
Administer tocolytic therapy (such as subcutaneous terbutaline) if contractions exceed 5 in 10 minutes or prolonged hypertonus occurs.
Perform fetal blood sampling (FBS) to obtain scalp pH and lactate when the trace remains pathological and prompt delivery is not already underway.

viva.q: What feature combination classifies an intrapartum CTG trace as non-reassuring?
viva.a: A trace having exactly one non-reassuring feature with the remaining two features normal is classified as non-reassuring (suspicious).

viva.q: What criteria place an intrapartum CTG trace into the abnormal (pathological) category?
viva.a: A trace is abnormal when it exhibits either one abnormal feature or two or more non-reassuring features, indicating significant risk of fetal acidosis.

viva.q: What time limit applies to decision-making when persistent late decelerations occur on an abnormal CTG?
viva.a: Action must be taken within 30 minutes, initiating intrauterine resuscitation and proceeding with fetal blood sampling or expediting delivery.
